_about: Study tips added by the study app (supplemental). General strategies summarise published learning research (sources below, links checked 2026-10-23); course tips restate conventions already in the lessons. None of this is instructor material.

sources.label: Dunlosky, Rawson, Marsh, Nathan & Willingham (2013), “Improving students’ learning with effective learning techniques,” Psychological Science in the Public Interest 14(1), 4–58 — summary from the Association for Psychological Science
The Learning Scientists — six strategies for effective learning (combining strategies)
American Statistical Association, GAISE College Report (2005)
Rohrer et al., interleaved mathematics practice (IES-funded project; e.g. Rohrer, Dedrick & Stershic 2015, J. Educational Psychology 107, 900–908)
University of Delaware meta-analysis poster: worked examples in mathematics (g ≈ 0.43)
Seeing Theory (Brown University) — visual introduction to probability and statistics

categories.title: How to study (what the research says)

tips.title: Test yourself instead of rereading
tips.body: Close the notes and try to produce the answer, then check it. Practice testing is one of the two techniques rated **high utility** in the Dunlosky et al. review; rereading and highlighting were rated **low utility** even though they feel productive. Try a quiz *before* you feel ready: struggling to recall is part of what makes it stick.

tips.title: Spread it out: short sessions over many days
tips.body: Distributed (spaced) practice is the other **high-utility** technique. With the final several weeks away, revisit each unit a few times on different days rather than cramming one long session. Returning when you have *partly* forgotten is the point; the effort to recall is what strengthens memory. The review queue brings back what you got wrong.

tips.title: Mix problem types once you know the basics
tips.body: On an exam nobody tells you “this is a binomial question”. Interleaved practice (binomial, then Poisson, then hypergeometric, …) forces you to **choose the method**, which blocked practice of one type never trains. Research on mathematics practice found interleaving improves later test scores. Block a topic while you first learn it, then switch to mixed sets.

tips.title: Study a worked example, then do one alone
tips.body: For new material, studying a fully worked solution first is more efficient than struggling from scratch (in one meta-analysis, a gain of almost half a standard deviation in mathematics). Then cover the solution and redo it yourself, and finally try a *different* problem of the same kind. Each lesson has worked examples from your lectures; each practice question has a step-by-step solution after you answer.

tips.title: Ask “why does this step work?”
tips.body: Elaborative interrogation and self-explanation (moderate utility in the review) mean explaining each step to yourself: *why* divide by n − 1? *why* is the median in both halves? *why* does subtracting Y add its variance? Few learners do this unprompted. Write the one-line reason next to a formula in your notes; if you cannot, that formula is a weak spot.

tips.title: Pair every formula with a picture
tips.body: Dual coding means combining words with visuals. A probability is an **area**; a variance is a **spread** you can see; P(X ≤ 3) is a set of bars. Sketch the distribution before calculating, or open the visualizer and move the parameters until the formula and the picture agree.

tips.title: Turn abstract rules into concrete cases
tips.body: Abstract statements (“the median is resistant”) stick better with a concrete case (“changing 5 to 50 in 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 moves the mean from 3 to 12 but the median stays 3”). For each rule, keep one small example you can recompute in your head.

tips.title: Statistics is about variability
tips.body: Almost every idea in the course answers one question: *how much do things vary, and what can we say anyway?* The standard deviation measures it, the IQR measures it resistantly, a distribution models it, and σ²/n tells you how a **mean** varies less than a single observation. When a formula seems arbitrary, ask what variation it is measuring.

tips.title: Build intuition by simulating
tips.body: The GAISE guidelines recommend using technology to build *conceptual* understanding, not just to compute. Draw a few hundred samples and watch: larger n makes x̄ cluster tighter; skewed data pull the mean toward the tail; R near 0 can hide a strong curve. Guess first, then run the simulation; the surprise is where the learning happens.

tips.title: Identify the model from its story
tips.body: Before any formula, write one line: “X = number of … , X ∼ …”. Fixed number of independent trials, count successes → **binomial**. Trials until the first success → **geometric**. Sampling without replacement from a small population → **hypergeometric**. Events in an interval of time/space → **Poisson**. Waiting time → **exponential/gamma**. Each lesson’s “How to recognize” list is exactly this.

tips.title: Translate words into inequalities carefully
tips.body: “At least 3” is X ≥ 3 = 1 − P(X ≤ 2). “More than 3” is X > 3 = 1 − P(X ≤ 3). “At most 3” is X ≤ 3. “Between 2 and 5 inclusive” is P(2 ≤ X ≤ 5) = F(5) − F(1). For **discrete** X the ≤/< difference matters; for **continuous** X it does not. Writing the inequality before calculating removes most off-by-one errors.

tips.title: “At least one” → use the complement
tips.body: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none). It is usually one short calculation instead of many. The same trick works for “not all” and for tails: P(X > a) = 1 − F(a).

tips.title: Check that the answer is possible
tips.body: A probability must lie in [0, 1]. A variance and a standard deviation are never negative, and a standard deviation is in the data’s units (variance in squared units). |R| ≤ 1. A mean should sit inside the range of the data. A 10-second check catches many arithmetic slips.

tips.title: Keep sample and population symbols apart
tips.body: x̄, s, R describe the **sample** you observed; μ, σ, ρ describe the **population** or model. Capital X̄ and S² are the sample statistics *as random variables* before the data are seen. Mixing them up is the most common source of n vs n − 1 and σ vs σ/√n mistakes.

tips.title: Quartiles: for odd n the median goes in both halves
tips.body: This is the class convention (Aug 31 notes). Software such as R or Excel interpolates and gives different Q₁/Q₃, so do not check exam answers with a default software quartile. The box-plot builder shows both.

tips.title: Fences are inclusive; whiskers ≠ five-number summary
tips.body: A value **equal** to Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or Q₃ + 1.5·IQR is an outlier (Site II: 1 sits exactly on the fence). Whiskers stop at the most extreme **non-outliers**; the five-number summary uses the **actual** minimum and maximum.

tips.title: Geometric and negative binomial count total trials
tips.body: In this course X ∼ G(p) is the trial on which the first success happens (x = 1, 2, …), so E[X] = 1/p. Some books count failures instead (x = 0, 1, …) — their formulas differ by 1.

tips.title: N(μ, σ²): the second number is the variance
tips.body: N(5, 4) has σ = 2, so z = (x − 5)/2. Standardize with σ, never σ². Likewise Γ(α, β) and E(β) use a **scale** β (mean αβ, or β).

tips.title: Discrete tables: P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a − 1)
tips.body: Cumulative tables give F(x) = P(X ≤ x). For integer X, subtracting F(a) instead of F(a − 1) drops the value a. The distribution explorer prints the F(b) − F(a − 1) step for every interval you choose.

tips.title: Variances add — even when you subtract
tips.body: For independent X and Y, V(X − Y) = V(X) + V(Y), and V(aX) = a²V(X). Square the coefficients; never subtract variances. The mean of x̄ is μ but its variance is σ²/n.

tips.title: Open book: build your own index now
tips.body: An open-book exam rewards knowing *where* things are, not having them. Star (☆) the formulas you look up most and use the **Saved** list as a one-page sheet; note the lecture page for each method. Practise with only that sheet so lookups are fast on the day.

tips.title: Keep full precision until the last step
tips.body: Rounding z to one decimal or s to two digits early can change the final answer. Keep calculator memory values, round once at the end, and write the unrounded intermediate on paper so partial credit is possible.

tips.title: Write the setup line first
tips.body: Start every problem with the model and the event, e.g. “X ∼ B(10, 0.3); want P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − F(2)”. It shows your reasoning, earns method marks, and catches a wrong model before you compute.

tips.title: Rehearse under exam conditions
tips.body: A few timed sessions with feedback held until the end show what you can do without hints — and are themselves retrieval practice. Note which topics cost time and send them to the review queue.
